title: SmartMed Help — 200 Cited FAQs
description: 200 original, source-supported drafts across general medicine, medicine-specific and personal/urgent questions. Personal and urgent records are clarification/escalation templates, not dose approval or overdose treatment. Coverage is selected, not a claim to cover all medicines or most patient questions.
coverage_note: Selected common medicines and salbutamol inhalers; no automatic coverage of other drugs, combination products, pediatric dosing, pregnancy prescribing or specialist regimens.

question_types.general_medicine: Use an applicable pharmacist-reviewed FAQ for general education.
question_types.medicine_specific: Match verified identity and formulation and use applicable verified clinical references.
question_types.personal_or_urgent: Personal questions need clarification and professional assessment; urgent concerns bypass ordinary matching and escalate immediately.

source_check_method: Supporting website content inspected during preparation; not pharmacist approval or an automated ongoing freshness check.
integration_status: Standalone handoff file; not installed, pushed or deployed.
population_note: Adult-oriented starter. FDA/NHS references are international; a Malaysian pharmacist must review applicability and local instructions. Do not extrapolate adult advice to children.
runtime_rules: Only retrieve entries enabled_for_patient_use=true AND review.status=approved_by_pharmacist; the supplied entries are all disabled.
Emergency or overdose questions bypass ordinary FAQ matching and use an approved local urgent-help flow. Do not delay help for identity clarification.
Require verified medicine identity for medicine-specific information. Apply existing LASA checks; never silently fix or guess names.
Match the actual ingredient, formulation and population. Brand aliases require verified product/country mapping; do not fuzzy-match a drug name into a confirmed identity.
Ask for required_context before individualized advice. Never replace a supplied prescription with a general FAQ.
Unresolved typed/photo conflicts block definitive taking instructions for the affected medicine.
Retrieve only relevant entries, not the entire library. If no entry applies, use approved clinical retrieval or pharmacist referral, not a forced FAQ match.
Render source links from the selected record. Never invent links or cite these sources for additional unsupported model claims.
An unidentified medicine makes a complete interaction review impossible; never declare the whole combination safe.
Keep original entered doses and uncertainty. A confirmation click is not professional verification of a concerning dose.
Translations into Bahasa Melayu and Chinese require separate clinical/language review before enabling.
Store originals and source metadata; respect source access/licensing terms. These answers are brief paraphrases, not copied monographs.
review_workflow: A pharmacist checks each answer, context restrictions, sources and local applicability.
Set review.status=approved_by_pharmacist and enabled_for_patient_use=true only for approved records.
Recheck changed guidance and sources; review translations separately.

faqs.question: What should I know before taking a new medicine?
faqs.answer: Know its name, purpose, dose, timing and important warnings. Ask your pharmacist to explain anything unclear before relying on the instructions.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Use Medicines Wisely
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I share my prescription medicine with someone else?
faqs.answer: Do not share prescription medicines. The other person needs their own assessment and instructions.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Use Medicines Wisely
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What is a generic medicine?
faqs.answer: A generic uses the same active ingredient as its corresponding brand medicine. In the US, FDA-approved generics must meet requirements for equivalent strength, form and performance.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Generic Drugs: Questions & Answers
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Why does my new medicine look different?
faqs.answer: Brand and generic products can look different. Ask your pharmacist to confirm the medicine, strength and instructions if its appearance changes.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Generic Drugs: Questions & Answers
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What should I tell my pharmacist about my other medicines?
faqs.answer: List prescriptions, shop-bought medicines and supplements, how you take them, and recent changes.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What allergy details should I tell my pharmacist?
faqs.answer: Name the product and reaction, such as rash or breathing trouble. Report previous reactions even if their cause is uncertain.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I cannot swallow my tablets?
faqs.answer: Tell your pharmacist. Ask whether a suitable alternative form is available; do not assume the tablet can be crushed.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I cannot read or understand my label?
faqs.answer: Ask your pharmacist to explain the directions in a language and format you understand. Do not guess the name or dose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I vomit after taking my medicine?
faqs.answer: Ask a pharmacist what to do for that medicine. Tell them its name, dose and when vomiting happened; do not automatically repeat the dose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Where should I store my medicines?
faqs.answer: Follow the storage instructions. Many medicines need a cool, dry place; some need refrigeration. Ask your pharmacist if the label is unclear.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Medication Safety Tips for Older Adults
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I leave medicine in a hot car?
faqs.answer: Extreme temperatures can damage medicines. Ask your pharmacist about the specific product if it was left in a hot car.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Medication Safety Tips for Older Adults
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: How should I keep medicine away from children?
faqs.answer: Keep medicines up and away from children, ideally in a locked place. Do not leave them within reach.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Medication Safety Tips for Older Adults
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I use medicine after its expiry date?
faqs.answer: Do not rely on expired medicine. Its quality or strength may have changed even if it looks normal. Ask your pharmacist about replacement.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Expiration Dates: Questions and Answers
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: How do I dispose of unwanted medicines?
faqs.answer: Ask your pharmacist about local medicine-return arrangements. Do not assume every medicine can be flushed or thrown into household rubbish.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Use Medicines Wisely
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I split my tablet in half?
faqs.answer: Ask your pharmacist before splitting it. Suitability depends on the exact tablet and its product instructions.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tablet Splitting
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Does a line on a tablet mean I can split it?
faqs.answer: A line alone is not enough to decide. Ask your pharmacist to check the product instructions and whether splitting gives the prescribed dose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tablet Splitting
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I split a slow-release tablet?
faqs.answer: Most slow-release tablets are not intended for splitting. Your pharmacist must check the exact product before you split it.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tablet Splitting
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I split all my tablets in advance?
faqs.answer: If splitting is approved for your tablet, avoid splitting the whole supply in advance. Split pieces may be affected by moisture or heat.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tablet Splitting
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What is a medicine interaction?
faqs.answer: An interaction happens when another medicine, food, drink or health condition changes a medicine’s effects. This can increase side effects or reduce benefit.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can vitamins or herbal products interact with medicines?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tell your pharmacist about every vitamin, herb and supplement so they can check it with your medicines.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Are shop-bought medicines safe with my prescriptions?
faqs.answer: Not always. Shop-bought medicines can interact with prescriptions. Ask your pharmacist to check the exact products together.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can two products contain the same medicine?
faqs.answer: Yes. Different products can contain the same active ingredient. Check ingredients and ask your pharmacist before combining them.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I drink alcohol with my medicine?
faqs.answer: Alcohol affects some medicines and can worsen side effects. The advice depends on your medicine, so check its leaflet or ask your pharmacist.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I take medicines while pregnant or breastfeeding?
faqs.answer: Ask your healthcare professional about each medicine, including shop-bought products and supplements. Suitability depends on the medicine and your situation.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Drug Interactions: What You Should Know
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Do antibiotics treat a cold or flu?
faqs.answer: Antibiotics treat certain bacterial infections. They do not treat viruses that cause colds and flu.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Antibiotics
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I use another person’s antibiotics?
faqs.answer: No. Only take antibiotics prescribed for you. A healthcare professional needs to decide whether you need them.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Antibiotics
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: How should I take my antibiotic?
faqs.answer: Follow your prescription or dispensing label and the medicine leaflet. Ask your pharmacist about unclear dose, food timing or treatment length.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Antibiotics
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I miss an antibiotic dose?
faqs.answer: Check the leaflet for your exact antibiotic or ask your pharmacist. Do not use a general FAQ to choose the timing of a replacement dose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Antibiotics
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What allergy symptoms need emergency help?
faqs.answer: Trouble breathing, throat tightness or swelling of the face, lips or tongue can signal a serious allergic reaction. Get emergency help immediately.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Antibiotics
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I stop atenolol when I feel better?
faqs.answer: Do not stop atenolol without speaking to your doctor. Your condition could worsen, and stopping may need a planned dose reduction.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atenolol
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I drive if atenolol makes me dizzy?
faqs.answer: Wait until dizziness, tiredness or vision problems have gone before driving or using machinery. Discuss persistent symptoms with your pharmacist or doctor.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atenolol
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I drink alcohol while taking atenolol?
faqs.answer: Limit alcohol because it can increase side effects such as low blood pressure. Discuss your usual drinking with your pharmacist.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atenolol
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I take more atenolol than prescribed?
faqs.answer: Seek urgent medical advice now; extra atenolol can be dangerous. Take the packaging and dose details with you. Do not rely on a chat answer.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atenolol
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I have grapefruit with atorvastatin?
faqs.answer: Avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice because it can increase side-effect risk. Ask your pharmacist about grapefruit and your usual intake.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atorvastatin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I drink alcohol with atorvastatin?
faqs.answer: Avoid excessive alcohol because it increases the risk of liver problems. Tell your pharmacist or doctor if you drink heavily.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atorvastatin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What is atorvastatin used for?
faqs.answer: Atorvastatin lowers cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. These are general uses, not confirmation of your prescription’s purpose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Atorvastatin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can rifampicin change the colour of urine or tears?
faqs.answer: Rifampicin can cause orange-red or brown changes in body fluids and can stain soft contact lenses. Ask about changes that worry you.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Rifampin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Should rifampicin be taken before or after food?
faqs.answer: General capsule guidance is on an empty stomach. If your label says something different, ask your pharmacist to confirm it before changing timing.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Rifampin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I take paracetamol with a cold-and-flu product?
faqs.answer: Check whether the cold-and-flu product also contains paracetamol. Combining products containing paracetamol can cause too much to be taken; ask your pharmacist.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Paracetamol for Adults
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Is the same liquid paracetamol volume always the same dose?
faqs.answer: No. Liquid products can have different strengths. Check the concentration and use the instructions for your exact product.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Paracetamol for Adults
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What does twice daily mean?
faqs.answer: It means two doses in a day. It does not tell you the amount per dose. Ask your pharmacist to confirm the timing for your medicine.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What should I bring to my pharmacist?
faqs.answer: Bring your medicine packaging, a list of all medicines and supplements, and details of previous reactions. Include how you actually take each medicine.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Tips for Talking with Your Pharmacist
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Is my dose correct?
faqs.answer: A general FAQ cannot confirm your personal dose. Show your pharmacist the exact medicine, strength, form and prescription instructions so they can check it.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: FDA — Use Medicines Wisely
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: I took too much medicine. What should I do?
faqs.answer: Seek urgent medical advice now, even if you feel well; effects can be delayed. Keep the packaging and dose/time details. Do not make yourself vomit.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Poisoning
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What is amoxicillin used for?
faqs.answer: It treats certain bacterial infections, including some chest and dental infections. Your prescriber confirms your reason.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I take amoxicillin with food?
faqs.answer: It can be taken before or after food. Follow any specific instructions on your dispensing label.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — How and when to take amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I chew an amoxicillin capsule?
faqs.answer: Swallow capsules whole with water; do not chew or break them. Ask about alternatives if swallowing is difficult.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — How and when to take amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: How do I measure liquid amoxicillin?
faqs.answer: Use the supplied oral syringe or medicine spoon, not a kitchen teaspoon. Confirm the prescribed millilitres.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — How and when to take amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I stop amoxicillin because I feel better?
faqs.answer: Finish the prescribed course unless your clinician changes it. Stopping early can allow the infection to return.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — How and when to take amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if my infection worsens while taking amoxicillin?
faqs.answer: Tell your doctor if you worsen at any time or have no improvement after 3 to 5 days.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — How and when to take amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can amoxicillin cause nausea?
faqs.answer: Yes. A meal or snack may help. Ask your pharmacist if nausea persists or is troublesome.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Side effects of amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if amoxicillin causes severe or bloody diarrhoea?
faqs.answer: Stop taking it and seek urgent medical advice. Do not simply treat this as a minor side effect.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Side effects of amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I get a new rash on amoxicillin?
faqs.answer: Contact a healthcare professional for assessment. Breathing trouble or throat swelling needs emergency help.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Side effects of amoxicillin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can amoxicillin interact with warfarin?
faqs.answer: Yes, the combination needs checking. Tell your pharmacist; monitoring or treatment changes may be needed.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Amoxicillin with other medicines
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I take amoxicillin with methotrexate?
faqs.answer: Ask your prescriber or pharmacist to check this combination before use because interaction problems can occur.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Amoxicillin with other medicines
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Are herbal supplements automatically safe with amoxicillin?
faqs.answer: No. Evidence is limited. Give your pharmacist the exact supplement names for assessment.

sources.title: NHS — Amoxicillin with other medicines
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What does metformin do?
faqs.answer: It lowers blood sugar and is commonly used for type 2 diabetes. Your prescriber confirms your treatment purpose.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Should metformin be taken with food?
faqs.answer: It is usually taken with meals. Check your exact formulation and follow your prescribed schedule.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can metformin cause diarrhoea or nausea?
faqs.answer: Yes, stomach upset is common. Tell your pharmacist if symptoms persist or bother you.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can metformin affect vitamin B12?

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What if I have vomiting or diarrhoea while on metformin?
faqs.answer: Contact your clinician for advice or follow your agreed sick-day plan because dehydration increases risk.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I stop metformin when my blood sugar improves?
faqs.answer: Discuss this with your doctor first. Stopping can let blood sugar rise again.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: NHS — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can I crush extended-release metformin?

faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Why is there a tablet-like shell in my stool on extended-release metformin?
faqs.answer: It may be the empty tablet shell, not a missed dose. Confirm the formulation with your pharmacist.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: What should I tell the clinic before a scan with injected contrast?
faqs.answer: Tell them you take metformin. Ask for exact stop and restart instructions; do not decide these yourself.
faqs.applicability: General education only; not an individualized dose or diagnosis.

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Can heavy drinking cause problems with metformin?

sources.title: MedlinePlus — Metformin
sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.

faqs.question: Why do I need kidney checks while taking metformin?
faqs.answer: Kidney function affects safe use. Keep your blood-test appointments and follow your clinician’s advice.

sources.purpose: Supports this educational answer; not patient-specific verification.
